statement: A row has 20 seats, numbered 1 to 20. Seats 8 and 15 are already taken. A family of four wants four empty seats next to each other. How many different blocks of four seats could they choose?

choices.misconception: I cut each stretch of empty seats into separate groups of four that do not overlap, instead of sliding the block along one seat at a time.
I thought there are $20 - 4 = 16$ positions for a block in the whole row instead of 17, then removed the 8 blocked ones.
I thought only 3 blocks contain each taken seat, so I removed 6 blocks from 17 instead of 8.
I counted every block of four in the row and forgot that seats 8 and 15 are taken.

hints: Which runs of empty seats are there between the taken seats?
Split the row into runs of empty seats. In a run of n seats, a block of four can start at any seat that leaves room for three more, so slide it along one seat at a time.
The empty runs are seats 1 to 7, 9 to 14 and 16 to 20, of lengths 7, 6 and 5.

solutions.reliable: The empty seats form three runs: 1 to 7 (7 seats), 9 to 14 (6 seats) and 16 to 20 (5 seats). A run of n seats holds $n - 3$ blocks of four, one starting at each seat that leaves room for three more. That gives $4 + 3 + 2 = 9$ blocks. The transferable idea: count by sliding a window one step at a time, and a window of length k fits $n - k + 1$ times in a run of n.
solutions.elegant: The whole row has $20 - 4 + 1 = 17$ blocks of four. Each taken seat lies in 4 of them (the blocks starting 3, 2, 1 or 0 seats before it), and no block contains both 8 and 15. So $17 - 4 - 4 = 9$.

whyOnTest: Sliding-window counting tests the off-by-one rule n - k + 1 and the urge to cut a row into separate pieces instead of sliding.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
